utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. For the next witness, there was -- were objections from the Prosecution to have the 92 ter statement admitted into evidence, and just to cut matters short, mainly because it's -- it's rather expert evidence than evidence of a witness of fact, at least in some of these paragraphs. Meanwhile, the Chamber has received a supplemental information sheet in which at least sources are mentioned of certain data. Who on behalf of the Prosecution will deal with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I'm dealing with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does the supplemental information sheet change anything in the objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: It actually does. Number 4 and 5 on the supplemental information sheet for MM-017, there's an explanation about paragraphs 16 and 17 and a reference to D420. Mr. Kuzmanovic entered this exhibit, D420, on the 25th of June, 2008 through Ambassador Galbraith. When I received this supplemental information sheet yesterday evening, I looked at the page references given at number 4 and 5, 3D00-1291 and 1292 and realised that, in fact, what's been uploaded as the English translation of this document is not the same as what the Croatian version of that document is. So, in fact, what he's relying on is only in B/C/S at the moment, and it calls into question the whole translation for --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: -- D420. So that's a simple thing. And just while were on the topic of translations, initially we received Mr. Pejkovic's statement in English, and it was printed off, and I've been working off that copy -- and I only raise this, Your Honour, because -- well, there's two points. Number one, I know Your Honour and the Bench in general rightly demands a certain degree of preciseness. What was filed in the 92 ter motion is actually a different translation in English as well with no notification to the Prosecution that that had been an updated translation. So what I've been working off of does differ slightly in terms of how the sentence structures are, et cetera. So even for the filing that we did in response to the 92 ter, we were working off the old translation. The paragraph numbers are the same, but it is troubling when we don't get notice that translations are being replaced with new translations. The number one on the supplemental information sheet is -- as well, Mr. Pejkovic indicates that paragraph 4 of his statement comes from the 65 ter 3D00723. Looking at that range - I think that was also identified in our motion. However, I just wanted to point out that one of the items on the potential exhibit list is 65 ter 3D00843, which is, again, an updated version that actually fills in the rest of that chart with new numbers and presumably that relates to number 7 on the supplemental information sheet, wherein Mr. Pejkovic indicates that in his -- the data in his statement relating to tables and numbers come from a database. So presumably that's what he has been using to generate these numbers. And, again, the Prosecution's position is that that is another demonstration of his expertise and a further indication that this isn't transparent; we don't know anything about where these numbers are coming from, how they're being generated. And so we would ask that 65 ter 3D00843 also be another one of the items that Mr. Pejkovic not be permitted to refer to during his testimony. And given number 7 on his supplemental information sheet, we also have issues with paragraph 11 and paragraph 8 because if he is saying that he generated the numbers from database, that is problematic. There's also an indication here that was disclosed apparently in another case over six years ago. I wasn't here then. I didn't know anything about this. And there's no notice other than what I got last night from the Markac Defence. I haven't had a chance to open that because what I did find in the system is just that it consists of a number of -- diskettes somewhere. I don't have access to that. And just the last point, number 8: Mr. Pejkovic indicated that he was supposed to be testifying at the OTP's request in the Milosevic trial -- again, I got this last night, so I've done what inquiries I can with the Case Manager on that case as well as with one of the other lawyers that worked on that, and they had never heard of Mr. Pejkovic. So I don't know anything about that. And then lastly, just in number 7 again: I don't know or on what basis he has any information about when things were supplied to the OTP and RFAs, et cetera, but that is another matter. Anyway, those are the issues that were raised by that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This witness was never designated as an expert, and this witness is not an expert. This witness is a fact witness. The OTP has been aware that this person has been a fact witness since we filed our witness list in May 2009. With respect to the translation issue, which I believe is a side issue, what CLSS provides, if that's different from the draft translation, It's not something that we do. It's not something that we are aware of. We provide a draft translation in our 92 -- in our 65 ter submission; all that stuff goes to CLSS; it comes out; it gets translated however they translate it; it gets uploaded into the system. I don't know how that works, but that's the system, and that's the system that we're dealing with. So whether there are any slight differences in what the translations may be, I'm not aware of. I'm working off of the CLSS translation, not off of the 65 ter translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you ever provide the draft translation to the other parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When we filed our 65 ter list in May, we provided them with draft translations which had not been translated by CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it clear that at a later stage you used the final translations. Is that something the OTP should have known?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You know what, Your Honour, I'm not aware of that. I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is not an awareness question. It is a normative question. Should they know?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure they should know; it's in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's a simple and short answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... You should know because it's in the system. That's a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We had the same issue with the first protected witness where a key word was mistranslated that we weren't aware of, that no one else was aware of. We had the same issue with the date of a witness statement which was so obvious that it was one date and it was translated as another date. So those minor mistakes for us are troubling because obviously we are relying on CLSS to provide an -- I mean, if we also have to read the translated document again from CLSS to ensure that it's accurately translated, that's just a huge workload for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, if you receive, at an early stage, a draft translation, is it visible that it's a draft translation not a CLSS translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You know, I can't tell that you off the top of my head, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's, of course -- that is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can talk to my Case Manager and let you know, but I don't know off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because awareness of possible changes depends on awareness of the provisional character of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The draft report is what we filed in May, and the corrected version of the -- or the CLSS version is what we filed with the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is not an answer to my question as you certainly are aware of. Can you see, from the draft translation you provide -- can you see that it's a draft so that you should be at notice that perhaps if, later on, a final translation is there that there may be difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, Your Honour. I didn't ask that of my Case Manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, often we see, in grey -- see we draft or provisional translation you can use that shadow-type of printing technique which we often see as a matter of fact. Is that visible in one way or another on the draft?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will let me co-counsel just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The initial translation does note that it's a draft translation. And when CLSS translated -- translates the document, there is an additional notation, which we don't provide, which is on the bottom of the statement. For example, in the 92 ter statement, if you look at the bottom of the first page in English, and I don't know if the Court has that. If we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we have is 3D04-1913-ET, 0/B -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. That shows that the document has been translated. At least what we are aware of from CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If I can just correct Mr. Kuzmanovic on one point. He says that the first one indicated it was a draft. I'll provide a copy to Your Honours if you'd like. It doesn't say draft on it anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it somewhere at the bottom, because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I just looked at it, no. It doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the first thing is that Mr. Kuzmanovic will now tell you where you can see that it's a draft. If you put it on the -- Could it be put on the ELMO so that we can see ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have that with us right now, so I can't answer that question. Every single translation that we've sent to -- in our 92 ter or in our 65 ter submissions were not final translations. They aren't final until CLSS says they're final.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that was not my question. My question was whether it was visible from that one that it was a draft rather than a final.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was told by my Case Manager that it was visible. I'll check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, give me one page of -- the cover page. If have you one, then we could have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Waespi just stepped out to get a copy. So if we could take a moment, and we could put it on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently you have noted there are some differences. Is this -- does it affect the substance? Not to say that we should not be very precise, but at the same time, of course, primary concern is how to proceed, whether we can do that on the basis of what you've seen, or whether you claim that we can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- just given -- I understand how important it is to be precise, and it is very difficult in these circumstances. For instance, just as an example, in the translation, the first one: Instead of saying 8.000 Serbs left during Flash; it had 80.000 Serbs. Different structures have been moved around in terms of wording. And then obviously when you get this -- when I finally figured this out yesterday when I was just trying to match up pages in order to be precise and realised that the one that was uploaded in the system was, in fact, different. And it was obviously a problem for me. I just -- I'm not confident that I'm in a position to cross in a way that would not create a lot of stop and go. So, I mean, if you were to be finished in chief today and just had some time to make sure and go through it. The problem is you prepare, you prepare, you do a summary, you work off of what's been provided - there's no indication that it's a draft - and then on the day before to find out that it's different is troubling. And it does create huge difficulties when you're trying -- when the questions have been drafted. I need to go back through all the questions. I tried to do that to the best of my ability, but I'm not confident that I've been able to do it, unfortunately. It is difficult to cross-examine someone and put precisely what they said and have to go back and figure out whether you have to change everything. And I just haven't had a chance to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you're both masters this morning and judging on the matters I raised but not answering my questions. I asked you whether you claim that we can't proceed, and I took it from your answer that you said, Well, let's see what happens in chief, and then it's all cumbersome, it's all problematic. That's clear to me. Can we proceed with the examination in chief in view of you -- apart from what will happen after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I think in conjunction with the mistranslation with the fact that, as I indicated, D420 is not correct either which is also something I was working heavily off of. It was on their exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll come to D420. But on the basis of what --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I think together it makes it -- it basically makes it virtually impossible for me to cross today, confident that I can refer to the documents that are going to be relied upon that were relied upon, according to Mr. Pejkovic as of yesterday, documents that we, in our filing, identified as potential sources. And then again, I haven't had a chance to go back through the filing either, Your Honour, to make sure that that is fully accurate, given that D420 was referenced. I don't know -- I haven't had a chance to have anyone do a new translation of that or have a look at the translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: You understand the point, obviously, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand the point. I also understand that your position is that do you not feel that you would be ready to cross-examine the witness on the basis of what you have got until now but whether that changes through the day or by tomorrow is still to be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes. And it would also depend, obviously, on the outcome of the Prosecution's motion on this statement as it stands now. I don't know where that is going either. So that may have an impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next point, D420, Mr. Kuzmanovic. That seems not to be just a -- is it just a translation issue, or is it that -- I mean a different text in English sometimes is apparently another translation of the same original, and sometimes it is because the original is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: The original is different. The numbers are different. And even the bottom of the first page of D420 says April 2000. That's the date of the document. The numbers that Mr. Pejkovic is relying on and that he's referenced -- and if you look at the pages he's referenced in the B/C/S, those are updated as May 2000. So unless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's already in your responses, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... right. Well, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is what I say -- yes, but I saw -- for some documents already that you say, Well, we have problems there because it is covering the different time-periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Expect what I realised when I got the filing last night, the supplemental filing, and specifically numbers 4 and 5, on the supplemental filing, when I looked -- when I first looked at the English translation, I was trying to find knows pages. And then I realised they were B/C/S references. I looked at the B/C/S references, and I saw that the charts that Mr. Pejkovic reproduces in whole that were identified in the -- in the OTP's objection to the statement actually are found in the B/C/S version, and they are updated to May 2000, which is not the case in -- in the English translation as it stands. So it is a different document. Obviously when you get it at 5.30 last night and you look at it, not speaking B/C/S and it's a 50-page document, I have no capacity to accurately go through and figure out whether the wording's the same. I mean, the numbers are different and the wording is presumably different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, here the issue is raised not as an updated translation but just a different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The translation, Your Honour, I have been informed has been done, and it is going to be uploaded today into e-court. Mr. Pejkovic can obviously tell the Court regarding his information and what he received regarding the database that's located partially in D420. I was also informed by my Case Manager that the updated translation of the Rule 92 ter statement was in May of this year, meaning that the document was available since May of this year. The official filing that we made 12 days ago -- this wasn't notice that counsel received yesterday or the day before. The official filing of the 92 ter statement was 12 days ago. So that's the document that we're going to work off of in our examination-in-chief. We did not receive any objections regarding this 92 ter statement till after business hours on Friday. So, obviously, we had to look and see what had this was all about. The first time it was raised specifically as to what the Prosecution was objecting to was after business hours on Friday. I let Mr. Waespi know that I wasn't really happy with that kind of notice, given the fact that the witness was potentially to start testifying on Friday. But, obviously, we went over the -- we went over the issue with him and provided the supplemental information sheet as a means to try to resolve, since we don't the time to file a formal response the issue related to this witness. On the 9th of September it was downloaded, the official translation, September 9th. So it's not an issue that this just happened Friday, or Thursday, or whenever. So with respect to the notice issue, you know, a simple phone call or simple discussion either before or after court would have been very easy to deal with. Instead we got a motion, you know, late Friday night letting us know that this witness is actually an expert and we're objecting to various portions of his statement. Obviously the supplemental sheet was provided in an attempt to deal with that issue in a timely fashion so that this witness can go forward today. I wanted to let -- advise the Court with respect to the Prosecution's motion. As I said, this witness is a fact witness. He will testify about his own work and the work of his office. This witness is not getting a -- an outside party getting a set of documents and interpreting them. He was intimately involved as the head of Office of Expelled Persons and Refugees in dealing with this issue from December of 1991 all through September of 2005. The data upon which he will testify comes from the database which was provided in its entirety to the Prosecution. You can ask Mr. Pejkovic that yourself. I personally saw the letter. Geoffrey Nice, he has that letter with him, Your Honours, the letter from the Prosecution going back and forth asking for this information. When Mr. Nice asked the Croatian government for who would be the witness -- or who would be the person or office that we'd need to contact regarding this information, it was Mr. Pejkovic. So if the Trial Chamber wanted to call a witness on this specific issue and ask the Croatian government, Please provide us with a witness who would testify on these issues regarding refugees and returns, Mr. Pejkovic would be the person who was designated. The -- as I stated earlier, the database was provided, the entire database, to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2003. I would like to add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was some dispute about whether the witness was requested to testify. From what you are now telling, should I understand paragraph 8 to be the following: The OTP requested that data would be given and the name of a potential witness provided to the OTP? Is that -- or was there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have the letter in -- or the witness has the letter in B/C/S, Your Honour. I don't know if he brought it with him today. We can -- we have no qualms about producing that letter so the Court itself can see what exactly was requested. Mr. Pejkovic himself told us yesterday during the meeting for the supplemental information sheet that he was requested to testify at the Milosevic trial. So -- and it was in conjunction with production of the database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now whether he would testify as an expert or as a witness of fact, is that -- you haven't seen the letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There is no specific request that he testify as an expert in any letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is he personally addressed, or is it the government who is addressed to provide --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There's both, Your Honour. There's both. Because since he was the person charged with this job and with the database, it eventually went through the Croatian government in a RFA and then directly to Mr. Pejkovic in a form of a letter from Mr. Nice, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We'll have a look at that. Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I hope -- I'll ask -- we'll see if the witness brought the information with him. If he didn't, we can get it at the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we move to the -- Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to -- if can I be assistant with respect to D420. In the original Croatian and in the English version, they both say they're from April 2000. So to me it seemed like there was a suggestion from the Prosecution that the English is a different document and says April while the Croatian must be a document that is after April. And, in fact, they both claim to be from April 2000. The second is that from my -- just from looking at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just then -- because if there's dispute about that, let's have a look. The original uploaded as D420 gives as the month and - forgive my pronunciation - is as the "tavanj."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Travanj" is April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, it's R -- "travanj." That's April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There was one other point, Mr. President. Then Mr. Carrier can respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It looks to me like the English translation of this is the actual Republic of Croatia contemporaneous translation. Because if you look at the English translation, it first of all doesn't look like a typical one done for the purposes of this case. And, secondly, in the left hand column, you see what appears to be a binding or a binder and that it came out of an original binder. So if there's an issue with the translation, it looks like both the original and the English are both original Croatian government documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although apparently the one uploaded as a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It appears that way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Carrier, let's try to keep matters simple. April. April.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I don't speak Croatian, so I was just going by the fact that the numbers were updated from May. If you just look at, very specifically, what he is referencing in his supplemental statement, those -- one of those pages, and if you look at the corresponding pages in the English translation, you see all the numbers are different. Whether or not the rest of the text in the 50-page document is different, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, data from an April 2000 report, could they cover anything which dates from May 2000 as well? Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. My Case Manager was addressing something to me. I will look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What Mr. Carrier says it's not D204 because it covers a time-period which is beyond April 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: D240, you mean, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the new one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D420. I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: 420, we all had it wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's Monday morning. That's no excuse, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, Your Honour, I can't tell you that without -- without -- we can ask the witness that, but off the top of my head, I can't tell you without having all the stuff in front of me. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next issue. Let's focus on paragraph 18: expert evidence, opinions. Let's read: "On the basis of these data, it is evident that the Republic of Croatia did not prevent the return of the Serbian population which lived in Croatia before the war." Mr. Carrier says this is opinion and this is not fact. And that he has -- let's just focus on 18 because that seems to be the -- for you, Mr. Kay, the most striking example in your view of expert evidence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, it's the summary and the words based on these data which now has indicated he has also compiled from the database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 18, objected to because it is expert evidence rather than evidence of a witness of fact. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the issue here is whether or not this witness can make a conclusion based on the data that his office compiled. I don't think that's an expert issue. We've had testimony from many other people in this case, and I can at this of a specific exhibit right now involving the chart that was used for evidence of destructed -- destroyed and burned houses, P421. There was a lot of information in that chart in which the people who were testifying concluded that there was a great deal of burning and looting going on based upon that chart's analysis. And now all of the testimony came in, and non of those people were expert witnesses. On the contrary, in this particular instance, Mr. Pejkovic is the person whose responsible was to deal with refugee, refugee returns, and the like. And I think a simple statement in his first sentence is -- is probably, if you read the statistical data, self-evident. And I don't think it goes into the realm of expert testimony at all. For example, we had Mr. Theunens who was an expert. He was an outside person who came in and reviewed all the documents and then made opinions based on the documents. Here this is the not the case. This witness was involved in compiling these documents; he did this work on a daily basis for almost 14 years; and it is very relevant and a factual issue for this witness to be able to make a statement like he did in the first instances - I will slow down here; I think I'm going too fast - of paragraph 18, I think, is quite relevant. And it doesn't go into the realm of expert testimony. We also had, for example, the list of dead bodies, P421. That was another issue in which there were objections. And the testimony came in about that list, and that was used as an example of either the Croatian government failing to do anything about it or the Croatian government condoning it. So I just wanted to use those examples, Your Honour, to take one sentence in the first sentence in paragraph 18 and claim that that automatically somehow makes this person an expert witness, I think, is -- is the wrong avenue. This person dealt with this database, compiled this database, worked with it on a daily basis for 14 years, and I don't think there is any other person in terms of witnesses that can come close to the level of knowledge and experience with respect to this issue on a factual basis than this witness. And that's our position on paragraph 18, Your Honour. And I might add that, you know, obviously if the Prosecution doesn't think that this statement has any validity or any truthfulness to it -- or not necessarily truthfulness but has some issues to deal with, it can be dealt with to probe his credibility and his knowledge in cross-examination. That's the whole point of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is not immediately in a position to compare all this. This brings me back into my mind the issues of Mr. Sterc, where the Chamber took it on a -- on a paragraph by paragraph basis. utterances.text: And you were ...

utterances.text: Your Honour, it is obvious on this document -- there is no specific designation on this document that was filed in May that it's a draft translation. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're repeating what you said before. I specifically asked you this, Mr. Kuzmanovic, and then you, at that time, confirmed, page 6, line 14, which was a mistake then, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the best thing I can do is to refer the parties to transcript pages 21.130 up to and including 21.133. And I'll just read small elements of that. "The Chamber previously considered that parties are not necessarily precluded from eliciting opinions from fact witnesses, that clear lines cannot always be drawn between fact and opinion, and very simple statements can also include elements of both. When a fact witness offers an opinion as part of his testimony, the Chamber considers whether that opinion has a factual basis in what the witness has personally experienced and whether the witness needed any special knowledge, experience, or skills in order to substantiate it." I then continued by saying: "In determining whether a piece of evidence can be admitted, the Chamber further considers whether the evidence predominantly consists of opinions or facts. However, when a witness provides opinions or conclusions that are of an expert character, that is, they're required that the person providing them has some sort of specialized knowledge, skill, or training, the Chamber expects this witness to provide this expert opinion in full transparency of the established or assumed facts he or she relies upon and the methods used when applying his or her knowledge, experience, or skills to form his or her expert opinion. Whenever possible, the parties should be given the opportunity to test or challenge the factual basis and methodology on which the expert has reached his or her conclusions." And then it continues with the minimum degree of transparency required. The Chamber takes the view at this moment that we find ourselves in a situation where it cannot be said that the statement is one purely of a witness of fact. And whether or not the 92 ter statement can be admitted or not, will be decided by the Chamber, after we've heard the evidence. So to see whether, at the end, the statement or parts of the statement do meet the requirements for a witness of fact and if some opinion evidence slipped in, whether that then fully meets the requirements. Apart from that, it has not been presented as an expert report, but if there are elements of expert evidence in there, whether it meets the requirements which apply when we're hearing expert evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What was and what is the time assessment for this witness? I don't know whether the present situation has changed anything in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's ask Madam Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Where, if the Chamber recalls, and I know it's been a long time ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that we went with quite some detail into how these numbers --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, of which the text is now being handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pejkovic. Please be seated. Mr. Pejkovic, you'll be first examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac. But before we do so, I'd like to return the initial statement to the Prosecution. From your answers, I take it, Mr. Kuzmanovic, that there is no need to verify whether I had the same document in my hands as you had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There is not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pejkovic. Before we begin, you have a binder in front of you. Can you tell the Court what it is?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's my statement and official reports from 1995 and 2000 that I need, because there are so many numbers that I cannot recite them off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, if Mr. Pejkovic should use these documents, I would always first turn to the Court and ask for permission for him to look at a document. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, for the record, tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Lovre Pejkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm currently a member of the board of a private business, Markson Investments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, do you remember giving a statement in our law office to this Defence team on the 11th of May of this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can I ask for document 3D00893.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You will see your statement now, Mr. Pejkovic. Could you identify your signature and confirm that it was the statement you have given to the Defence team of General Markac?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Last page, please, so we can identify the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC

utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I take it that the objection stands. And it follows from the ruling of the Chamber earlier how to proceed that this document will be MFI'd and a decision on admission will be delayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, be so kind and tell the Court how your professional career came to be linked with the office in which you worked from 1991 through 2005. Could you describe your career?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: In November 1991, the then deputy prime minister, Dr. Mate Granic invited me, together with another group of people to a meeting and asked me -- asked us to organise an Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees of the Republic of Croatia which, by virtue of the decree of the 22nd November, 1991, was indeed established. And as part of my work obligation, I started to work in setting up this office from the very first day. I remained in it until the 20th September, 1995. I cannot see the transcript in front of me. Could it be switched on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Mr. Pejkovic, to facilitate our communication, we need to make a pause between questions and answers. You said you stayed there until the 20th September, which year?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: 2005. In that time, I discharged various duties. But I became a full-time employee on the 1st of December, 1995, as a senior advisor. My next position was chief advisor. And then I became deputy chief of that office. And finally, on the 30th of May -- sorry. 30th January, 1996, I became chief, which I stayed -- and later, when it was incorporated into the ministry, I -- I became deputy head of ODPR, and I stayed there until the 20th September, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We see that it's a government office. Tell us about its position in the executive authorities. What is the position of that office relative to the executive authorities?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the person superior to that office, the immediate superior, is the deputy prime minister. And above him stands the prime minister. At the beginning, it was Dr. Mate Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is the main function, the mission, and the purpose of establishment of that office?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose was to provide care and accommodation for all displaced persons and refugees who, at that time, in end 1991, found themselves in Croatia. I have to say that there had been, even before, a system of social security in Croatia that contributed from the start. But the refugee and displaced persons crisis was of such a scale that it required a special body that would have immediate contact with the government in resolving the serious problems facing Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What mechanisms were at the disposal of the office? I mean, human resources and material resources as well as the legislative background.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a decree on the status of expelled persons and refugees; the decree under which the office was set up that was in end 1991. On the 15th of January, 1992, the Sarajevo cease-fire was agreed. The arrival of the UNPROFOR into Croatia was agreed. And we all felt that the end of the war was not far, and it would put an end to the occupation of our occupied territories. And the expelled persons, those who had been expelled from Croatia, would very soon, the next spring, be able to return to their original areas of residence. At the binning, there were no big investments into the organisation and equipment of the office because we did not think at that time that it would need to exist longer than the summer of 1992. However, now in hindsight, we all know what actually happened. The UNPROFOR arrived; the state of occupation was cemented; and during the man date of the UNPROFOR which was primarily to return the refugees to their homes, another 12.000 persons were expelled. More than 600 persons who remained in the area were killed. And not a single expelled person returned. All these things that I said a moment ago placed new demands on our office. And pursuant to government decisions, all the available accommodation for tourists on the Adriatic coasts, all hostels and hotels for our employees, all temporary accommodation for builders and workers was turned over for refugees. In 1992, the aggression and occupation against Bosnia-Herzegovina started, and that created a exodus of its population, Bosniaks and Croats and Muslims, via Croatia, so that towards the end of 1992, at one point, we had 750.000 persons expelled either from other areas of Croatia or refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that moment, Europe stepped in to help resolve the humanitarian crisis. And a part of refugees, primarily from Bosnia and Herzegovina, were accepted by various European countries to that our number stabilised around 450.000 displaced persons and refugees in the care of the Republic of Croatia. To deal with this, the office had a personnel of about 80 staff and another 200 assisting, through 103 social security centres in Croatia. So around 280 persons were more or less directly involved into the process of caring for refugees and displaced persons. That does not include all the NGOs that arrived in Croatia at the time to help with this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Keeping records of such a great number of people was rather complicated, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a very delicate and very difficult task because it was not only about counting them, it was about identifying people and enabling parts of their families, away from Croatia, to find out where their families were, enabling them to either reunite either in Croatia or in a third country, which was primarily a humanitarian issue. And then, information about their numbers: where they were accommodated, their status, their age group, all this information was needed in order to organise normal schooling. We have to say that not a single child missed a single school year in Croatia. Everybody was able to continue schooling and to enjoy free-of-charge health care. You understand the organisational difficulty this involved but also the financial difficulty. We had to organise extra censuses, the first one of which was in 1992. And, at that time, we counted 247.271 expelled persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just a second, excuse me for interrupting you. But tell us where were these data recorded; what did a refugee file, to call it that way, consist of; and where was that kept?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: For each person who was covered by the census --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I apologise. I just -- he got cut off. I was actually interested to hear about the different censuses and how they were compiled. Is there any -- he got cut off there by Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I suppose I am allowed to conduct direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, your question was rather broad whether it was -- whether keeping of records of such a great number was complicated. That, of course, asks for a rather broad answer as well. But I think you're entitled to -- if the answer goes into the direction which you're not heading for, that you cut off the witness. At the same time, we know that Mr. Carrier then at a later stage will ask the witness about these data. So therefore, for the understanding of the evidence, it would be advisable if we would hear that from the witness now. But I'm not -- you're not under any obligation to do it, but you're invited to let the witness finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Pejkovic, I have to look at the record again, because I forgot what I asked you. The question was how was this huge collection of data archived, and how did a basic file of each of the expelled person look. And how was it organised? I was interested in the technical aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic. Witness, when you started explaining about the census where you - because I heard the first figure of 247.000 - where you actually more or less repeating what we find in paragraph 4 of your statement in which you refer to the census of expelled persons in April 1992, the refugee census in March 1993, the census of expelled persons and refugees in June 1994, and the re-registration of expelled person, returnees and refugees in March /April 1997. Is that what you wanted to refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I was just going through my direct examination towards that goal and towards that explanation. And I have in mind, and I will go through it with the witness, but just in a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, then, the best answer to Mr. Carrier's objection would have been, I'll deal with all the details in my next questions. Then Mr. Carrier would immediately have sat down. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic, what I wanted to know before we move on to my next question was what was the methodology of recording the information about the refugees and how was it all processed in the technical sense?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: When we had a census, we listed families. And for each family there was a family sheet in which individual information for each family member were recorded. And we had a set of about 80 answers that we wanted to collect with each such registration. Each expelled person received an identification card with a photo, and that was his personal identification. The information was processed by being entered into a database.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say "a database," do you mean physically, that you had archives where those cards were collected? Or do you have something else on your mind as well?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: To be clear, we had a database in the sense of archives where the files were held in hard copies, but there was also an electronic format database that we had in a computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, what was your personal role in connection with the database and the systemisation and the handling of this database?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: I started working in the office after being the director in charge of the automatic data processing in Ljubljanska Banka, a bank that was operating in Zagreb at the time, and I am and have been a professional who was in charge of organising this kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us now return to the issue of the numbers and the figures which you mention in paragraph 4 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And before that I would ask the Registry for 3D00843. In a second we will see this document on the screen, Mr. Pejkovic. And, in connection with that, I will ask you for an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I could ask one clarifying question to start with: You talked about family sheets, 80 questions, and, therefore, I take it 80 answers on those sheets. Now, were they filled in by the family members themselves, or were they interviewed and was the family sheet completed by some official person? Could you tell us how that was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, an authorised person who was interviewing the expelled person providing the data would collect the answers, and if the person had any personal identification, and then some of the data was copied from them, and eventually the person would sign it, because it was a kind of statement in which the person provided all information about himself or herself and their family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I believe we have Sanction on, Mr. Registrar. Yes, that's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic, now you can see a table. If you look at the Croatian version, it says, at the top: "Registered expelled persons and refugees in the Republic of Croatia from 1991 to 1995, compiled by Lovre Pejkovic." Mr. Pejkovic, are you the author of this table?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what was the purpose of compiling this table and how did you compile it?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: This table is the result of all the reports which were published, beginning in January 1992. And practically, to this day, they are still being published each month. And in order to present all this to the government and to the international community, every month, towards the end of the month, we would provide statistical data in a report that showed the number of expelled persons and refugees who were accommodated in the Republic of Croatia. And this is actually the sum of the figures from our statistical database.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we now return to paragraph 4 of your statement. And when you said that in April 1992 the total number was 247.278 expelled persons, so almost 250.000, I can see in the table in the columns for 1992, the month of April, that the number is 247.278 expelled persons. So is this the piece of information that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And likewise, Mr. Pejkovic, according to other data that you mention in point 4 of your statement, when you talked about year 1993 and further on, do you also make reference to the information from this data which you compile yourself?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wish to tender this table into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I raised this objection this morning, and I object to the use of this document for precisely this type of reason. I'm confused because on the supplemental information sheet, D1826, which has been MFI'd, Mr. Pejkovic said that, in paragraph 4, the data that he's using there actually came from a different document, which is 3D00723. Now Mr. Mikulicic has shown him this document which he said he produced and that's where he got this data from. And, again, this goes back to the whole problem that we don't know how this data was collected. What he is actually referring to is not transparent. And it's not clear exactly what the methodology was to produce it. He produced that chart or he produced the one in 3D723 [sic], but I object to the admission of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could easily go to clarify that questions on a -- let's say, more time-consuming way. And, therefore, I would kindly ask the Registrar the document that Mr. Carrier just mentioned 3D00723.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, what Mr. Mikulicic suggests is that before the Chamber decides on admission and on your objection, that he, by some further questions, will clarify the issue which are you have raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. I was just -- I was waiting for the ruling itself before we kept proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will delay the decision on admission and will first hear the further questions Mr. Mikulicic will put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could I please see on the screen the document 3D00723.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us in a few sentences what this is.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is one of the reports that the office issued, or published, and this is it a report from July 1995, which was sent to the Government of the Republic of Croatia as a report for approval and adoption with the proposal of certain measures which would be taken afterwards in order to provide care to expelled persons and refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was this report approved and adopted by the government?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there another addressee, apart from the -- Government of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: This was a public report for general use. This was distributed to all representatives of the international community. That was why an English version was also produced. And it was then distributed to the embassies to the Republic of Croatia, the NGOs, the monitoring missions that were present in Croatia at the time, and not let me not list everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will have around ten minutes' questions referring that report, so if maybe that would be a convenient time to take a break before my next line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a convenient time to take the break. The break will be a little bit longer due to technical problems. We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Your Honour, I apologise. Before we leave, I have one general question that I would like to ask of the Bench to ask of the Prosecution and why it was not -- why wasn't the database and the information related to the database and the fact that this was witness was sought as an OTP witness in a different case relate to us in any Rule 66(B) or 68 disclosure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, could you -- it seems that where you said you verified that and nothing was known, apparently there was some correspondence. Perhaps we should ask the witness whether he has the correspondence with him and give you, then, an opportunity to verify that during the break and then to see what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: In that respect, obviously, I got notice of this last night and I -- as I said before, I did what I could. So we just -- at this point, no one has any information on him being a potential witness for Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I think Mr. Kuzmanovic, at this moment, is not claiming any bad faith on your side personally but would rather have a response, a Prosecution response, irrespective of any personal shortcomings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you, Mr. Pejkovic, We do understand that you have been in contact with the Office of the Prosecution as a potential witness in the Milosevic case. Is there any correspondence you have with you at this moment which would confirm that? Would you be willing to give us -- well, not the Chamber, but to give a copy so that Mr. Carrier has an opportunity to review that -- you get your original, you will get that back. But that at least we can copy it so that Mr. Carrier can prepare an answer to a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just so I'm perfectly clear, there is no written request for him to be a witness. He was asked telephonically to be a witness. The documentation he has is regarding the database. And then, after that, he was requested to be a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any further -- Do you have any further details -- from whom did you receive a call for the purpose of exploring the possibility of you appearing as a witness in the Milosevic case; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I received a call from our Office for Cooperation with this Tribunal, and I responded to this invitation. Mr. Osorio, who is the representative of the OTP in Croatia, asked me in the presence of our head of office whether I was willing to testify in the Milosevic trial, which I accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not a telephone conversation, but it was a direct conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was face-to-face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in the presence, as you said, the head of your office. That was Mr. Osorio. Do you remember when it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think sometime around the year 2000. But I am not certain. If I had been preparing for that, then I would be able to check it in my files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it before or after Mr. Milosevic was arrested and transferred to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was before Mr. Milosevic's arrest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Carrier, does this give sufficient -- And could you show us -- if you would be willing to give a copy of the letter so that we are better able to see what happened at the time. If would you give that to Madam Usher. Then we will have now first a break. And as I said before, we need half an hour. We will resume at five minutes past -- no, apparently we are not yet at that point. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so you know, all the documents are in B/C/S, so none of them are in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I take it that if these are letters that Mr. Carrier will find someone who at least has some understanding of what the letter says. Isn't it, Mr. Carrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if I could have the letter referred to on page 12 by Mr. Kuzmanovic from Geoffrey Nice, as well, which he said he saw personally. If I could just have that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give all the letters you received from The Tribunal in view of a possibility that you might be called as a witness. If there are more letters, we would like to have them all -- or at least Mr. Carrier would like to review them all. We will have a break, and we will resume at 10 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have had a chance to look at some of the letters, not all of them. There is -- I think because LiveNote was down, there was some confusion about handing them over to us. So, I did the best I could, but I still need more time to go through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't expect you to immediately -- but it seems that at least there is some correspondence in which this witness is specifically addressed not to say as an invitation to be a witness but at least there has been some correspondence which -- the Chamber received a copy. We didn't ask for it. But since we got it, we had just a glance at it. Nothing more, nothing less. Mr. Mikulicic, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am Your Honour, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Pejkovic, before the break, we saw that report from July 1995 on the screen. Can you tell us, in two sentences, what it is about and what your role was in drawing up this report?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: The report was made in order to inform the Republic of Croatia and the public on the status of expelled persons and refugees at that moment in the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What part did you play in drawing up the report?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: As one of the leaders of analytical section within that office, practically generated all the tables from the database, and they form an integral part of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will ask you to help us define certain categories mentioned in this report. The same categories that are often referred to in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move to page 3D03-0269 and in English 3D03-0309. It is a few pages further on. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, here in this report, at the very beginning, certain categories are defined. So I would ask you if could you just briefly inform the Bench about these definitions. How is the category of expelled persons defined, according to this report?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: The displaced persons are citizens of the Republic of Croatia who were banished by the ex-JNA, and rebelled Serbs from the occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia, or persons who fled from the Croatian-occupied areas because of demolition of their homes, terror, shelling, and other war consequences. So they fled to another part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And returnees are defined how?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: The returnees are the persons who returned to their homes. But we must know, as I mentioned, that there was a separation zone. But in the depth of territory behind the separation zone, there was a huge number of demolished houses, and the people who fled that area became displaced persons. But with the coming of UNPROFOR, the reconstruction began. So they returned to other areas of Croatia into their homes which were now reconstructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How would you define refugees?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: According to the Geneva Conventions and its Additional Protocols. On the one hand, those are Croatian citizens that had fled from the Republic of Croatia into third, let's say, European countries. But also foreign nationals who fled to Croatia, fleeing from the war and immediate threat to their lives. In this case, citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina who fled to -- to Croatia. That is, also Croats from Yugoslavia which was, at that time, Serbia and Montenegro, and Kosovo, who also fled to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And finally we have the category of refugees in transit which is self-explanatory but still ...

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Part of the refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina managed to secure admission by European states. But to get there, they had to be pass through the Republic of Croatia because that was the only possible free passage towards Austria, the Netherlands, Germany. And in Croatia, they could get to the embassies where they would take care of all the paperwork necessary for admission into a third country. And they would spent in Croatia a month or two because -- and they were thus in transit. We did not have to take care of them for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In all these categories of people, your office took care of all of them?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How was it financed?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: The office was financed by the government through the budget and through humanitarian aid that arrived. It was partly institutionalised. For instances, the European Union assisted through its ECHO programme, and that was aid in food. Various European countries provided financial aid through reconstruction and maintenance of refugee centres, such as Switzerland, Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, let me not enumerate all the countries. But this was never more than 10 per cent of all our budget spending for refugees. We practically needed 550 million dollars per year, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, let me try, in order to avoid that I'm misunderstanding the evidence. Do I understand that where you asked "expelled persons" and the witness answered, at least it was translated, as "displaced person," that expelled persons/displaced persons, that's one category which, where apparently the word "prognanika" is used. Is that the same category, expelled or displaced?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Category "prognanici" is -- is category "displaced person" in -- in English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But we could ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time -- at the same time, if I look at paragraph 4, first bullet point, I see -- and that perhaps has created the confusion. I see that it is translated as expelled persons. And your question was translated to us as about the category of expelled persons, how they were defined - page 41, for me, line 16 - and the answer then starts with: "The displaced persons." Apparently expelled and displaced is used in a similar sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, then, and I'm now addressing the witness, do I understand that the expelled or displaced persons that a category of people that moved within the internationally recognised borders of Croatia; whereas, you call refugees those who came from outside Croatia? Is that the main distinctive element in the definitions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is a fact that there is a terminological confusion when we speak of refugees and displaced persons. The term "displaced person," "prognanik," is now in use. Prognanik is identical to displaced. The confusion comes when we translate it into English. Do we use properly displaced or expelled, expellee? Whereas, refugees are those who came from a third country into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the category refugees is different? That is "bjelice" which, then, is those coming from outside of Croatia to Croatia. I wanted to clear this up right in the beginning, otherwise we will have a totally wrong understanding of the evidence. I think it is clear to me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic, you said you kept records about that as well. What was the ethnic structure of the population of displaced persons and refugees?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking of the total population of displaced persons and refugees, the majority were Croats, because, in the occupied territory, practically all the Croats who lived there --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And according to the 1991 census --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. I wanted to stop before. My understanding in the beginning was that Mr. Mikulicic was going ask permission of the Bench first before the witness read, and I noticed he was just reading, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't notice that. But if is he reading from a hard copy of the same document, but please ask him, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic, now when you are talking about ethnic structure, you are referring to the 3D -- page that ends with 0271. 3D03-0271, of the Croatian version. And 3D03-0311 in English. That's a part of the report that deals with this subject. It's better for the Trial Chamber to have the statistical part of the report before them.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: There were over 93 per cent Croats among displaced persons and refugees, around 2 per cent -- just over 2 per cent Serbs. That includes Serbs who did not agree with the Serb aggression and who were also expelled from their places of residence which they had shared with Croats. It's a changing number, and we can discuss daily movements as we monitored them in our database. But a person looking from outside can wonder what kind of numbers are these. They keep rising and falling. Yes, because some people were coming and others were leaving. Some people were displaced persons in Croatia and then found alternative residences in European countries. Some of them returned from European countries and back to Croatia and became displaced persons again. So, yes, there were daily movements, and we monitored them, and included that in our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move on to Croatian 3D03-0274, and in English 3D03-0314.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, could you tell us a few words about the status and the rights of displaced persons and refugees listed in this report. You see this on the screen. Give us a brief comment.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Under the decree on the status of displaced persons and refugees that later became law --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... is on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm just -- I still have concerns about the reading. I notice that he has his book, Mr. Mikulicic did say he was going to ask permission. I didn't hear permission being granted. If he is referring to us on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But I do understand that what actually happened is that Mr. Mikulicic did put questions to the witness and he earlier said that, in view of numbers, he would need to consult documents and that he is quoting from this same document, which is on our screen at this moment. And that became, at least, clear to me. We earlier, the page we saw earlier was page 5 of the -- page 5 of the English translation of this report and e-court numbering. So I take it that at this moment that the witness is telling us about this document which is a document underlying some of the data which we find in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So, then, on that note, perhaps it is not necessary to have a book open. And I can see from here there's handwritten notes on paper, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are any handwritten notes, then you are invited to close them and only to look at those documents we are aware of that you're looking at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarification, I could ask the witness what is this handwritten notes that he has in front of him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you can ask him to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... page of that document so it has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as long as I do not know what is written, then, it could be anything. If you want to ask him, you can do so. And why he thought it relevant to -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, I can also see that on the left empty page of the document there's something handwritten. What is it?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: I wrote a reminder for myself, that, in 1992, the UNPROFOR arrived. Their principal mandate was to ensure a cessation of hostilities and the return of refugees. However, during their tenure, not a single refugee returned. Around 600 persons were killed, those who had stayed in occupied territories, and an additional 12.000 persons were expelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you write this before you arrived in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it sounds almost literally the same as your testimony earlier today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I prepared last night for giving evidence, and while doing that, I looked through the background material and made a few notes so that I can focus on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please not consult any further notes, unless we are aware of it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Pejkovic, on the screen in front of you is a part of the report from 1995 which talks about the status and rights of displaced persons and refugees. I would ask you to explain to the Bench what was their status and what were their rights, and where did these rights and the status come out from?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: The government of Croatia had just pass as decree on the status of displaced persons and refugees, which was later turned into a law by the parliament. The displaced persons and refugees had right, the right for the necessary accommodation. And for this reason, practically all the vacant rooms in hotels and other tourist resorts were used for this purpose. Then they had organised meals provided to them. Also, financial assistance, in particular, for those who were accommodated privately with their families. And of the total number, which was between 400- to 450.000 refugees, some thousands were accommodated in an organized manner, whereas the others were staying with their families. Then they also had the right to free health care, the right to education, the right to humanitarian aid. And there were also special categories of those who were in need; for example, persons who had been exposed to sexual violence. They had the right to social psycho-social assistance. Then all earlier detainees or prisoners who had spent the greater part of their time in detention or in camps, whether it was in Serbia or in Montenegro, there were -- they were also provided with a social and psychological assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As for the extent and scope of assistance that was provided to displaced persons and refugees, was it equal to everyone in these categories, or was there a difference concerning their ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: No difference was made on the basis of either of the criteria that you mentioned. There was only a difference as to whether someone was a citizen of the Republic of Croatia or not, and certain other rights followed from this, and these rights are regulated differently in every country. But as for the basic rights, which I mentioned, everyone was equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have mentioned that certain obligations to this category of people followed from international legal documents.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Croatia fully implemented the Geneva Convention on refugees and the Additional Protocols. Even before Croatia became independent and was recognised, we invited the UNHCR to come and help us and instruct us and train us so as to deal with everything that was new to us. This was aggression where we had to take care of thousands of people, and we asked for help. And I must say that the first office of the High Commissioner for refugees was next to my office in the same building. And from the first day, we cooperated with them; they assisted us; and together, we were doing this. This was the first time that something like this was happening in Europe, this great movement of the population. And we were resolving this together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
