utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, your line of questioning seems to move away from what we see as a 92 ter statement and also the relevance of -- apart from one or two questions you put to the witness, seems to be rather small. And the Chamber further wonders whether there's any dispute about whether those who were displaced within Croatia, well over 90 per cent being Croatians, whether they were taken care of properly, health care, et cetera, and whether there was any problem in status of refugees and whether the Conventions were applied properly. Is there any dispute about this? And I'm talking about those who were displaced within Croatia before Storm and Flash --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May I answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'm asking whether there is any dispute about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May I answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm first asking Mr. Carrier whether there is any dispute about these facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could I answer now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My intention was first to depict the Chamber broader context of these events. And second, to be frankly, Your Honour, I'm not aware what facts are in dispute what facts are not in dispute because this question is ongoing category in this proceeding. So something that was in dispute ten days ago, now it is not. And vice versa. So to be on the save side, I am doing like this. But I will move from that topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, still, it's unclear exactly what was in dispute as far as you refer to what was two weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The intention of the Croatian government as it refers to the question of refugees and the expelled persons as it concerns to their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said one or two questions were relevant that. Was exactly the one I had in mind, whether any distinction was made between Serbs and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Croats. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the question that the Chamber asked is a good one, given there is some question as to what the position of the Office of the Prosecutor is on this issue. It has this case where it does or presents months of evidence concerning what happened in Operation Storm but has very little or takes no account of what happens on the efforts made to return. And, frankly, I know that within the Defence, and I'm sure the Chamber shares this, there is some confusion as to see what the Office of the Prosecutor's position is with regard to these individuals. And in discussions with my colleagues, and we've all shared this concern, that is why we have raised this. And this is come up at various times. And it's a direct result from the lack of clarity on the position of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not only a good question by the Chamber, but it isn't even a question that has been answered by now. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will do so, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic, you mentioned the role of UNHCR, and we'll talk more about that later on. Now I wish to return to a part of your statement in which you refer to exact data, which we can find in paragraph 4 of your statement where, for example, you mention that the census of displaced persons conducted in April 1991 is either the result of 247.278 displaced persons. The question was asked whether this number came from, so I will ask to you explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But, before that, if we could see, within the document we have on the screen, the page in Croatian 3D03-0286, that is to say, in the English version, page 3D03-0326.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, we can see tables in front of us. They're an integral part of this report for the year 1992 and 1993. That's what is on the screen right now. Can you tell us what was the methodology when composing these tables? And as for the information in the tables, did you use them when you were giving the statement to the Defence team of General Markac?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: The data that we can see on the screen are the result of the data processing from the database. This was permanently followed and occasionally we made censuses because this population was such that it was constantly on the move. So all the data which I can see in front of me now were used when we talked during the interview in connection with the Defence of General Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And your personal role in producing these documents was what?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was to organise the census, then to process the data, and to present the data in the tables which were then integrated in the reports. One of the reports is this one from the month of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, when compiling these tables, did you add any -- it's difficult to formulate this without formulating a suggestive question. Did you add any of your ideas, or was it simply a technical list of data collected on the ground?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: This was just a collection of the data from the ground. I must say that all the data is something that the OTP also has. All the data was provided to the OTP. And by a simple method, the Prosecutor can find the same data that you can see here in the table. Not on the basis of tables but of individual data which we submitted to them. We submitted 1.070.000 items. That was in 2003. And each item had about 80 attributes from which the same data can be drawn, the same data that we arrived at in 1995 and included in this report. I must say that representatives of the Prosecution visited our office. They also inspected our files. That is to say, the dossiers that you asked about. At the time we had 703 metres of files, that is to say, the family sheets that contain all the individual data, as well as the entire correspondence pertaining to each case were included in the individual files. All of that was offered for inspection. And I'm saying here under an oath that there was no manipulation with any data. I also wish to inform the Honourable Court that in 1997 we worked on the reregistration of the displaced persons and the USA bought the computer system and donated it to the office, and the office established a direct link to the UNHCR to this database. So since 1997, the UNHCR, as the leading UN agency for refugees, has direct access to our database.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now that we have data from 1992 on the screen, I wish to ask you to focus on the month of April. The figure mentioned here is 247.278 displaced persons. That is the figure which you mention in your statement in paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the result of the census which was conducted at that moment in the month of April for the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would ask you something about this report, Mr. Pejkovic. What were actually the two main problems of the crisis with displaced persons and refugees that your office was faced with? What were the problems relating to the occupied territories, the possibility of return, and also considering the standard of accommodation and the status of displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when this report was drawn up, the population of displaced persons was dissatisfied with the developments and the lack of possibility to return. Areas of Croatia were still occupied. The UNPROFOR was in these areas. The displaced persons began to form associations. They became, in a way, a political force which was openly expressing its views and became a partner to the government and other political factors and wanted their return to be enabled as soon as possible. It was normal that no one was happy about being displaced. You can never compensate anyone's home with any -- with anything. The government was faced with this dissatisfaction of the displaced persons, and it was also becoming a real heavy financial burden to finance all the displaced persons. And thirdly, the displaced persons were accommodated in hotel. For example a place like Opatija, which is a real tourist gem in Croatia, all hotels in that town were filled with refugees in 1995. So practically until that point hotels could not work normally. They could not be open for tourists. There were many complaints by hotel enterprises because they had lost profit. They wanted damages compensated, also compensation for the damage made by the refugees. They were threatening with lawsuits. They were asking for interests. And these were all problems about providing care to refugees and displaced persons in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have a number assigned to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'd first like to put a few questions in relation to the questions you put to the witness and some of his answers. You took us to April 1992, and you explained that the number of 247.000 displaced persons was the result of a census. Now, the numbers for January, February, and March, what were they then based on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the office had 22 branches across Croatia, which we called regional offices. They were doing their own statistics, and they sent it on a monthly basis to us at the central office. And on the basis of this data, we established the data included in this table. As I said, because of the fluctuation of this group of people, at one point we decided that a census should be conducted because we simply believed that the figures do not match the actual situation on the ground. It was wartime, and it was not possible to have reliable data at every given moment, but the data was as presented here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, what I'm looking at, that from March to April 1992, the number of displaced persons goes down by 110.000; whereas, in that same month, the number of refugees grows with some 175.000, which, I take it, is the result of reassessing the situation. Were there really such changes, or is it just a matter of classification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we are talking about the category of displaced persons, we did that census because we realised that this data from March do not reflect reality. And that's where we did the census. And the census established a lower number of displaced persons. However, as far as refugees are concerned, that was a moment of massive in-flow of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina to Croatia. And these are records showing how many people came into the Republic of Croatia that month and applied for refugee status which was approved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But were how were the date then -- well, let's say the 356, if I read it well, from March, displaced persons -- you earlier told us that registration took place on the basis of interviews, 80 questions filled in by a, what I understood to be a competent person, and then signed. How could that suddenly, well over a hundred of thousand, what went wrong either in the -- must have been something wrong in the registration, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We started registering displaced persons and refugees as they came in. At that time we did not have a personal identification card for everyone. People were simply registered. Now, when a person went from Zagreb to Rijeka, he appeared there practically as a new displaced person because he was not accompanied by a unified -- uniform identification number. Now, when we did the census, we found that the system was not properly functioning. It needs to be adjusted. And that's why this decision was made, to create a unified, integrated list of displaced persons. And this number, 300-something thousand, turned out not to be true, because many of them were simply off the records now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, the initial system of registration was not accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At the beginning, it was not accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you say that as far as refugees was concerned there was a huge influx of refugees. But could it be that, already in March 1992, that there were already far more refugees than registered, the 16 and a half thousand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, Your Honour, we did not -- we were not doing a re-registration of refugees. This figure for refugees was arrived at in the same way as the figure of refugees up to April. We just collected data about their registration through regional offices throughout Croatia. Only later did we start making lists of refugees in the same way as we did it for displaced persons. These were two independent jobs done at two different times. However, April 1992 was the moment, indeed, when a massive exodus of refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do you have an explanation for the big change in numbers in April 1993? There the number of refugees which drops by -- well, well over 110.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have these numbers next to me, but I think in 1993 we, again, did a -- a listing of refugees. That's how I explain this huge discrepancy, which occurs also with displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, it did not occur with displaced persons in 1993. Let me give you the numbers for March and April 1993. Displaced persons, March, 252.000; displaced persons for April, 250.000. So approximately the same, a slight variation. Refugees, March 1993, 386.000; April 1993, 269.000, a difference of some 115.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we made a census of refugees as such at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which then shows that the numbers were by some 30 per cent wrong before, as they had shown to be wrong in relation to displaced persons, similar percentage, in 1992? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. Until we started applying the same methodology that we used for displaced persons, we had this error with refugees, and you can see it from these numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there ever any census done any later, 1994 or early 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last census made was in 1997, when we did a complete re-registration of all displaced persons and refugees. And, at that time, we put in place a system of daily monitoring for every displaced person and refugee. Technically, that meant that every displaced person or refugee had to come in once a month --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me stop you there. I was interested in knowing whether a similar correction through a census would have taken place until mid-1995. These census, was that similarly 80 questions or -- I mean -- and was that on the basis of an interview, or did persons report themselves on paper? Could you tell us how the census was held technically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, technically, authorised persons took the census; whereas, displaced persons and refugees were invited to present themselves. The census took no less than one month. Among displaced persons and refugees, there was quite a large number of illiterate people who were not able to provide any kind of written statement. It had to be taken by an authorised person, a census-taker. It was read out to them, they would sign it, and they would receive a copy of this registration form for their own personal use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that include also some 80 questions, or was it more limited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Around 80 questions. We collected identifying information, information on ethnicity, faith, educational attainment, employment record, whether someone had been in captivity or not, sexually abused or not, what happened to other members of their family, whether they were alive, whether their whereabouts had been known, whether they had been killed, whether any family member was in a camp, their former address --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I earlier asked you about people being interviewed and having to sign for the result. Did you, at that time, refer to the census in your answer; or did you refer to the registration, which we find in this list not corrected yet by the 1992 census and the 1993 census for refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We always collected similar categories of information according to a list we received from the UNHCR. They had more experience, and they helped us make the questionnaires and develop a methodology of integrating that data. Of course, as time went on, we got more experience ourselves. We tried to improve on our own work and improve the quality of information we received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What now explains the rather big differences here and there where the registration and the census were apparently taken by competent people, not just self-reporting. Do you have any explanation as to why the registration went so much wrong and where the census corrected in such a -- well, substantial way, the outcome of the earlier registration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about the same people all the time. But even before the registration, they were registered in the census. The problem lay, however, with the central methodology of processing the data. Someone who lived for a month in Zagreb left then to Split but remained registered in Zagreb and was again registered in Split. That's how the numbers were artificially increased. If a person left a certain place, they were not taken off the records. They just appeared again in -- in records in another place. It would be the same as if I wanted to change my place of residence. I would have to de-register in Zagreb, in order to register in Split. If I don't do that, I appear as registered twice, in Zagreb and in Split. That's where the flaw was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any chance that we -- you would get benefits by not de-registering in one place and by registering in another place, that someone, displaced or refugee, would enjoy twice a benefit? Is that ... that is, I do understand a possibility, which ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is a fact that this possibility existed. In order to eliminate it, we moved to a different system of payment to savings accounts. Then, out of the total number of beneficiaries, which was around 190.000 persons receiving financial aid, we found 92 cases of abuse. With the new system, there was one savings account for one person. And when we integrated all the data and introduced a unique identification number for each person, it was no longer possible for people to get double benefits, as was the case before. There were 92 cases of such abuse, fraud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when was this new system introduced? Can you give us a year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So up to 1997, the registration was such that in order to get double benefits, that people might have registered more than one time. Thank you. Mr. Carrier, Mr. Mikulicic asked this document to be tendered into evidence. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1827.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think it has sufficient substance on its own not to be dependant fully on the admission of the 92 ter statement. Therefore, D1827 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic, let me try to wrap up this subject raised by the Honourable Judge. You were actually learning on the job. This was completely new to you?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the methodology of collecting and processing data, you necessarily find some disproportions and had you to adjust.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We reacted immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Honourable Judge pointed out significant discrepancies between months. In the course of 1992, 1993, 1994, until 1997, did they occur regularly to the same extent?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. This took us all by surprise. Nobody had expected aggression or the war, and there were no logistics to begin with for coping with these huge numbers. Do you know what 300.000 people means?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can I ask for D214 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, I will now show minutes from a meeting of the government of Republic of Croatia held on 5th of June, 1995, when did the decree on return of displaced persons and refugees to newly liberated areas was adopted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's 3D00-0688. That is to say, D214. And the page is 3D00-0688. 12

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the government, at its session, adopted a decree by which it regulated the return of displaced persons and refugees to the newly liberated areas? First of all, let me ask you if you're familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And secondly let me ask whether you participated in any way in the preparation of the text of this document?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the basic idea behind this document was to stimulate the return of displaced persons to their homes, because, as I said, the displaced persons had, by this time, already become a political force and requested some benefits for themselves, and now by the operations Flash and Storm the preconditions were provided for them to be able to return, and therefore a decision was made to organise this return, to organise reconstruction so that as soon as possible the displaced persons could return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the effect of this decree? What was the impact it had on the population of displaced persons and refugees?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was partly administrative. Because, on the basis of this decree, we cancelled the status of a certain number of displaced persons, especially to those whose homes were less damaged from the first to the third category, and those who received financial assistance so they could return to their homes. While, on the other hand, we had a situation that the entire liberated area could not receive all the displaced persons and refugees because of the situation there. So we had to take into account that if someone was returning and had children who were enrolled in schools there had to be conditions for the children to continue education. If we are talking about the categories of people who in need, such as the elderly people, whether they would have health care and social welfare provided, all of that was very difficult to secure at the time. And the results were not as the government expected, that there would be a return en masse and very quickly to the newly liberated territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You indicated you were closely cooperating with UNHCR. I will now show you a document, and that is the statement of Ms. Sadako Ogata.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that's D690, please, and if we could please see page 4 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, did you know Ms. Ogata. Did you have contacts with her?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will show you where Ms. Sadako Ogata, on 10th October, 1995, gave a statement in Geneva, quite an extensive statement about refugees, which had to do with the conference about the former Yugoslavia. We'll look at paragraph 2 on page 4 where she says that she must emphasise the importance of having internationally recognised humanitarian principles, and, first of all, it must be voluntary. The return must be voluntary. Mr. Pejkovic, we also -- implementing this internationally recognised humanitarian principle in your work with displaced persons and refugees [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: We always implemented this principle, that the return must be voluntary, that the person returning has to be well-informed what he will find upon return, and that the return must be safe and must be sustainable. These are the fundamentals which we applied and tried to implement in connection with entire population, whether it was internal displacement and people were returning to other parts of Croatia, or whether they were coming from abroad, or whether they were coming from Croatia into other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You anticipated partly some of my questions, but let's move through that briefly. Ms. Ogata says also that, in addition to the precondition that the return must be voluntary, she also says in the second paragraph that the return must be organised, and it has to take place in stages. She also says that she believes that were three stage, the first stage was the return of people displaced internally within Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The second stage would be the return of others from the former Yugoslavia. And the third stage would be the return of those who left for other countries. She means European and non-European countries. Were these principles which Ms. Ogata sets out herein, during the conference in Geneva in 1995, were they honoured?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Sorry, Mr. President. I just want to make sure that Mr. Mikulicic takes care not to lead on these points. If he could ask the witness what he knows about the different things before putting what Ms. Ogata says about certain things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are invited not to lead the witness in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, you mentioned, as one of the preconditions for the return, the issue of safety, the safety of returnees. Can you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't heard you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... problems with our earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I hear you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that one of the preconditions was also the safety of returning refugees who were going back. Can you please comment on that considering the situation in 1995 after the conclusion of Operation Storm in the newly liberated areas?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: In the newly liberated areas, in 1995, we immediately found out that some population had remained there. We conducted a census of them. And we established that there were around 10.000 difficult cases. These were mostly the elderly, the weak who had remained there; and complete care needed to be provided to them. They stayed in isolated areas because practically there was no public transportation available whatsoever. And I'm saying all this just to show you what the situation was like in this entire area. With the assistance the various governmental and non-governmental organisations, we provided for them, and the greatest probably was how to make sure that they would survive the winter, because they were alone without family members and without anyone who could help them. It was very difficult to work because practically the whole territory was vacated and devastated, and it was difficult to guarantee a great degree of safety or security to anyone and especially the sustainability of return at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now ask for the document 3D01-0841 to be shown on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, as for the persons who were refugees from the Republic of Croatia and who wanted to return in the second half of 1995, how could they do that at the time? What were the modalities for their return?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: As for the refugees who had left the Republic of Croatia, the possibility to return was connected with their possession of Croatian personal documents. Whoever had Croatian documents was free to leave the Republic of Croatia or enter it again without any problems. As for the persons who did not hold any Croatian documents, Croatia allowed humanitarian joining of families. Some of the families were separated because of the war, and one of the basic principles of humanitarian law was to enable family reunion. And, on the other hand, to provide assistance to difficult cases. These are the AVIs, in English, the elderly and the frail who had remained in Croatia to make it possible for their younger family members to return and practically take on, themselves, the care about their parents, brothers, sisters, their immediate family members, in other words. And in very short time we received a great number of requests for a return that was immediately after the Storm, that we started receiving these requests. The sources were various embassies that people contacted who then forwarded that to the government of the Republic of Croatia and the government forwarded it to our office. Then there was the office of the Government of Croatia in Belgrade, where the Serbs, who had fled, sent their requests, stating their wish to return. And there were also family members within Croatia who filed requests, asking that their family members be allowed to return to the Republic of Croatia. And there was the return of these people through the humanitarian principle of family reunion. That also started immediately after the conclusion of Operation Storm. Some of these people had taken refugee in Bosnia or Serbia. Some persons used the opportunity to leave to Hungary or Austria. They would then conduct our consolute or embassy. They would be issued with new documents and then returned to Republic of Croatia without any problem. But the majority of them were in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: An individual request for return could also be filed with international organisations in addition to the addresses that you mentioned, wasn't that so?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Our office cooperated closely with UNHCR, and any request could be submitted to the UNHCR, wherever it had an office, in Serbia or Bosnia and Herzegovina, or Montenegro, Hungary, Slovenia. There were UNHCR offices everywhere. And then UNHCR also had a network of NGOs that were working for it and practically visited refugees and offered them this possibility to apply for return. In Serbia, there was also the Serbian Helsinki Committee, which also worked a lot on making it possible for the refugees to return. That was among the refugee population within Serbia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that persons who also did not have Croatian personal documents could submit applications as you have described?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was nothing barring a person from submitting an application. Of course, the processing of applications was much easier and much faster if they also submitted identification papers together with an application. Because then it was possible to process it more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But what if they did not have Croatian identity papers?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: If they did not have them, then there was a possibility for them with cooperation with UNHCR. We organised go-and-see visits. Such persons could come to Croatia, visit their place of residence, see the state of their property, visit certain offices on the ground, obtain the documents that they needed. And all of this was organised together with our Ministry of the Interior, which provided security during these visits and allowed people to cross the border on the basis of lists that they had. They issued identification papers to such persons on the ground. And on the basis of this, once they returned, they could decide whether they wished to return or not. I must point out that in some municipalities in Croatia we had problems because the complete files had been taken away: the registers of births and of deaths, the registers of citizens, the land registries, ownership registries. And it was only around 2004 that some of these documents were returned to the countries, and then we could start working with this in the proper manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could see the clock. If I may have additional five minutes to complete this portion of my examination, that would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at transcribers, interpreters. Five minutes, Mr. Mikulicic. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic, you told us that the requests to return to Croatia could be submitted in various places, and you mentioned the office of the Government of the Republic of Croatia in Belgrade. No diplomatic ties had been established at the time. You can see now one such request submitted by Mr. Jovo Opacic. You cannot see what's at the end, but it was submitted in the month of February 1996 where he submitted the request saying that he wished to return to Croatia together with his family, his wife, son, two daughters, and his mother. Do you recognise the format of this form as a form that was in use at the time?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm personally familiar with this particular request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Maybe, if you could say just a few words so that the Bench would know Mr. Jovo Opacic. Who was he, was he a public figure?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a public figure. One of the co-founders of the Serbian Democratic Party. He was also for a while the president of the Red Cross in the so-called Krajina and, of course, his application for return was interesting to all of us especially his explanation as to why he wished to return to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm reading from what's at the bottom of the page. Mr. Opacic said that Croatia was his homeland, his native land, that was where the graves of his and ancestors were, and that together with his family he wanted to return there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we could turn, now, to the second page, we can see the attachment to the form where he addresses the Government of the Republic of Croatia through the office in Belgrade and where he states, on page 2 of this document, where he states that he had left Croatia with his wife and two minor children in 1995 contrary to his will, and that was part of the general exodus which was the crown of the pathological policy of Slobodan Milosevic and his Bolshevik branch office in Knin, with a goal to hide their own responsibility for the war in Croatia and to impose a new genocide against Serbs to Croatian people. Mr. Pejkovic, do you remember if this individual request for return was approved?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was approved and Mr. Opacic really did return to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could this document please be assigned a number, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1828.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Pejkovic, do you remember when the return was approved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell you precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometime, I think, in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any documentation, since the application is there, is there any documentation, Mr. Mikulicic, which would allow verification of -- of the further events in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try to find it, Your Honour. Out of the top of my head, I have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed. Oh I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do not proceed; that's my request. We will have a break, and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic, before the break, we were talking about the application to return by Mr. Jovo Opacic. Do you remember how many individual returnees there were in the last -- in the second half of 1995 and on in 1996? What kind of numbers are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about several thousand persons. I don't have the statistics before me. But the procedure was set in place by that time; people could make individual applications for return and family reunion; and they received approval to return. And on of basis of that approval, they crossed the Croatian border and returned to their families. That was just before the programme for the return of displaced persons and refugees was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that your office organised go-and-see visits dealing with individual returns. Could you explain what kind of visits these were, and why they were organised?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: I've said before at that one of the conditions for return is that it is of one's own free will. But their decision must be well-informed. In order for people to be properly informed into what conditions they would be returning, we organised, together with the UNHCR, these visits for potential returnees to come, view their property, see their families and friends, and find out first-hand about the situation into -- in places where they would be returning, get documents during that visit, return to their places of exile, and then make a final decision whether we wanted to return. We organised a great number of these visits, enabling individuals from larger groups to come and then inform their fellows on the situation. A person going on a go-and-see visit was not going for their own purposes only but in order to go back and return -- go back and inform another 20, 30, 50 people, so that they can make their own decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask for D682, page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, I'll now show you a report entitled: Human rights situation in Croatia, under UN Resolution, 10/19 from 1995. And the date is 5 March 1997. We will focus on paragraph 16. You stressed several times that the return has to be voluntary. Let us look at paragraph 16 of this UN Security Council report. I will quote it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... refugees in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of some 337.000 Croatian refugees now in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, roughly 35.000 (roughly 10 per cent) have expressed an interest in returning immediately to Croatia. It is believed, however, that this number would increase if conditions of personal and economic security for Croatian Serbs in the former sectors were to improve." From this report of the UN Security Council, we can see that, according to the 1997 census, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, around 10 per cent of refugees, expressed interest in immediate return to Croatian. Does this correspond to your information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to see where the 1997 census is, and I may have missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The report is from March 1997. The paragraph 16 says: "According to the data from the population census of refugees ..." So was really my conclusion that this census is from 1997, not from 1998 or 1999 because the report is previous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we could ask the witness perhaps. I don't know when exactly the 1997 census took place. Could you tell us when were the results known, Mr. Pejkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a census conducted in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It's not a Croatian census. It does include Croatian refugees in the territory of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so we're talking -- and we haven't seen any FRY census yet. I'm not asking for it, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I think I have access to a summary perhaps of that information which I can try to make available perhaps during my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you deem fit to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All in all, it's a question of UN report from the Security Council from March 1997, and credibility and exact of the figures that has been raised in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, I'm asking you, Mr. Pejkovic, if this number, around 35.000 people in 1997, who, according to the UN Security Council expressed interest in return to Croatia, matches your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Until that time, we received around 30.000 applications for return, including 14.000 applications for real return; whereas, 16.000, approximately, were property-related applications that did not involve actual return. This seems to correspond to this number here for potential returnees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to doubt these statistics?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't agree with this number, 337.000 people registered as refugees in the Republic of Yugoslavia. We never managed to agree about that number, and ultimately it was proven that it was not accurate, just as there was some inaccuracy in our own numbers that we later adjusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page to see paragraph 19, it mentions the agreement on the normalisation of relations between the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, signed in August 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's D412, already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It says here that the agreement, with the consent of the parties, Article 7, the parties committed to ensuring the return of refugees and displaced persons, including the return of their property or a just compensation. What did this agreement on the normalisation of relations do?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the commission entrusted with the implementation of this agreement and Article 7. And its most important effect on the population of displaced persons and refugees was that a protocol was signed on the organised return of refugees between what was then the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Croatia, enabling the return of everyone to their homes, with compliance with the basic principles. The voluntary principle, safety, and viability of that return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Pejkovic, that until the signing of this agreement in August 1996, there had been no conditions for organised return, only individual returns?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Individual return had always existed as such, but organised return, supervised by both governments, was not current until this agreement was signed, including this Article 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we could now see D428, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will show you, Mr. Pejkovic, a programme for the return and care of refugees and displaced persons that was adopted at the session of the Croatian parliament at the end of June 1998. Are you familiar with this programme, Mr. Pejkovic?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you, on the basis of your open experience and the work you were doing, tell what you say was the importance of the adoption of a Programme for Return?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: The Programme for Return was adopted after lengthy discussions and contrary opinions relating to the return, particularly the return of Serbs to the Republic of Croatia. However, those who adopted this Programme for Return were predominant in the end, and what was envisaged here was the return of all persons who were in the category of refugees, according to Geneva Conventions, so that they could return to Croatia once again by using their right to return in an organised manner. The return depended on an individual's free will. And on return, it was stipulated that all of them would be equal and everyone would have the same rights. If their homes were damaged, they had the right for them to be reconstructed. If their homes were settled by somebody else, then they were entitled to be provided with care until their homes were vacated. Again, they were entitled to financial aid and all other benefits that followed from this status. Practically with this programme, all Croatian citizens were now in the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we had a look at point 5 of this programme, which is on page 2 of this document, we would see that the programme was also coordinated with the representatives of the international community. And it is mentioned here which representatives theses were: the UNHCR, the UN DP, the UNICEF, and so on and so forth. Is it correct that your office, which was in charge of these issues, coordinated its work with these international representatives, or was it just something on paper?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: The implementation of the entire programme was to be done by the government of the Republic of Croatia through its offices and ministries and departments which took part in the implementation of the return. Those who provided assistance and monitored the whole problem was UNHCR, plus other organisations, the OSS, which was particularly in charge of security, as there were usually problems about the returns. So it was to report about the security issue. On the basis of this programme, every individual who was returning received a receipt about the plan for return, and the UNHCR was also provided with these receipts. So they knew for every individual when he or she would be returning, who had approved the return, or if not, why that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we could please see 3D00721.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have said that international community was present in one way or another. And now I will show you a statement by the president of the Security Council dated the 2nd of July, 1998, relating to this topic? Firstly, it is noted that the general security situation in the Danube area is relatively stable. And in the bottom part, it says the following, I will quote this in English: [In English] Examination welcomes the adoption by the Government of Croatia on 20th June, 1998, of a nationwide programme for the return and accommodation of displaced person, refugees, and resettled persons ... and calls for its prompt and full implementation at all levels, including the application of discriminatory property laws and the establishment of effective mechanisms allowing for owners to recover their property." Mr. Pejkovic, what was your experience from the time with the reaction of the international community to the programme for the return and also the conclusion of the agreement guaranteeing the return of private property that was concluded with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: The entire Programme for Return in the legislative part, which defines the procedures and processes for return, was written in cooperation with the international community. And this is why such an opinion of the Security Council was expressed because practically we had accepted and adopted whatever the international community requested at the time. And it was all implemented through the Programme for Return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would ask for a number to be assigned to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1829.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. When quoting the Security Council, Mr. Mikulicic, you have drawn our attention to the relatively stable situation. The quote starts with "therefore." The "therefore" does not relate to the stable situation but, from what I see in this document, refers to concerns expressed by Security Council on a number of matters which are explicitly mentioned. Since you did not read the "therefore," is it -- was it your intention that we should focus only on what you did read, or was it by mistake that you left out the "therefore"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I cannot follow you. I was quoting the sentence which begins: "The Security Council notes that the overall security situation in the Danube region is relatively stable."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I cannot see the word "therefore" here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... no. That's the previous paragraph to which you have given apparently some importance. The quote in the next paragraph starts with: "The Security Council therefore welcomes the adoption by the government on Croatia ..." And then the part you quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The therefore relates to the beginning paragraph in which the Security Council expresses grave concerns --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see your point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for a few matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I omitted by mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you didn't want not to draw --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, no. Not at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- attention to what preceded. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see the document D420 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, now we will see a document which is already in evidence. And this is a report on the implementation of the Programme for Return and care for the returnees displaced persons and refugees from the month of April 2000. My question is are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to note that I'm not sure what my friend is going refer to. But earlier today, Mr. Kuzmanovic notified the Court on record that it -- this document was being update. My understanding is that it has been updated with 18 pages on the end which consists of charts and text. In addition, during the break, given the other problem that was identified, apparently there are also portions that are in the English that aren't in the Croatian or B/C/S text either. So just to put on the record my concerns with the document globally at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly keep that in mind. And, of course, it's -- the Chamber cannot predict how Mr. Mikulicic will deal with it, whether he will pay specific attention to portions that come as a surprise to you or whether he would ignore those portions and focus on other matters. I do not know yet, and, therefore, let's first see how matters develop. But it is it on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Apart from the 11th standup of my learned friend during my direct examination, if my learned friend would have patience, then he will realise that I will go only through a couple of introducing pages in that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which are the same in the old version and the new version what from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's right. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, sometimes it takes some age to develop patience. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] If we could, please, move to page 3D00-1246 of this document in the Croatian version. And in the English version, it's page number 3D06-0102.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, before the intermezzo, you said you were familiar with this document, wasn't that so? Can you tell us what was your role in connection with this document?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the Programme for Return of displaced persons and refugees, a commission for the implementation of this programme was also established, and I was the chairman or co-chairman of this commission. And the result of the commission' work, was, among other things, the document which I see on the screen in front of me. So practically it was drafted under my supervision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, under number 1, it is mentioned what are the documents that are necessary for the return and that guarantee a return to all persons without any conditions or any waiting. If you see this list of documents, is there anything you wish to point out, in connection with these documents, that you noticed in your work at the office as being indicative in any way?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can just say that it is mentioned that there should be the operational procedures of return signed between the Croatian government, UNTAES, and UNHCR, which enabled the return of people to the Danube region. That is to say, the Eastern Slavonia. And by this, the peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia and the Danube region in the Republic of Croatia began, and in this document from the year 2000 provides once again the overview of the results of this mission, which was successful for the UN in the Eastern Slavonia region of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, tell us, what was the importance in the work that you were charged with, that is to say, the programme for the return of displaced persons and refugees. What was the importance of communication with neighbours, because here we are -- we see that the two-way return is being discussed. So which factors were important?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: These processes were never one way. They are, by their very nature, two-way processes. If we consider the situation which is easy to imagine: If I had come from Bosnia-Herzegovina and was staying in your house, and you had fled to Eastern Slavonia and you were in somebody else's house, and this person was waiting in Zagreb to return to this house. So without the possibility for everyone to go back to their homes, additional tension would be created. There would be a conflict between states, who did more, who did less, who was working faster or slower, who had more obstacles to return, and who had fewer obstacles. And I have to say that Croatia really did what it had to and not just what it had to, but eventually, with some resistance which existed, and which we must be aware of, this was adopted as part of the state policy, and it was regulated through laws, and we did really implement that. In addition to this, we managed to achieve that with constant monitoring from the international community and a great number of NGOs which were also monitoring everything that was taking place on the ground, pointed out to us our mistakes and errors. But whatever we were do, we were doing in good faith and a wish to enable everyone to return to their homes. Whenever a mistake was pointed out to us, eventually we did our best to overcome that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see page 2 of this document now, both in the Croatian and English versions. And I want to refer to a segment of the text in passage 3, talking about the procedures of the return. When I said the seconds page, I meant the next page. It's page [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] 7 in Croatian and 3D06-0103 in English version. So the next from the previous one. That's the one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see here that the Office for Displaced Persons was responsible for this, and that was your post, to put it that way, in cooperation with UNHCR, the Ministry of the Interior, and Ministry of Justice, as well as the administration and local self-government. What was the role of these two ministries in this process as well as the role of the local self-government? You have told us about the role of your office and the role of UNHCR, but can you please explain the role of these other bodies?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: The role and the task of the Ministry of the Interior was that, on the basis of a received application, it checked the status of a person as regards his or her citizenship and then to check if the person was in the criminal records. If that was the case, then we would address the Ministry of Justice to check what this was about so that we could inform the person who had submitted the application what kind of charges there existed and whether this person would be arrested by the police upon return to Croatia. And we wanted to avoid fear being spread through the population of refugees, that they were all on some sorts of lists and they were all accused of war crimes. I must say that some persons were really on the lists of persons accused of war crimes. We had several cases in which persons, after this kind of information, provided a written statement saying that they were informed they would be arrested when crossing the Croatian border but that they had not done anything and that, before the court, they would prove their innocence. And several such people did, indeed, return and did prove their innocence. I have to say that this was, of course, monitored closely by the international community, each such case, when there was such prosecution in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The registration and organisation of the return is described here. It is mentioned that the persons who had left the Republic of Croatia could submit the request for return to Republic of Croatia in which way. Under item 1, it's mentioned that they can submit it to the relevant diplomatic mission of the Republic of Croatia in a foreign country. The persons who did not have Croatian documents should personally contact the closest diplomatic mission. And then, under item 2, they could get in touch with UNHCR or the Commissariat for Refugees in Serbia or Montenegro or the Ministry for Refugees, Displaced Persons of Republika Srpska. This manner of applying for return was implemented previously in the Republic of Croatia, if I understood your earlier testimony correctly.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was applied even before. But the procedures that had been prescribed before were now written into the Programme for Return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last paragraph. And one more page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This paragraph deals with the return of Serbs from Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina that started back in end 1995, before the endorsement of the Programme for Return. Even then, there existed a procedure for those who did not have any documents to return for the purpose of family reunions. Part of such returns were not organised, and it was not officially monitored. During field checks, and in the course of the implementation of the programme, some of such returns were registered. But some returnees who had not yet registered yet had to be. It is the estimate of European monitors and UNHCR that there are around 20.000 unregistered returnees between 1995 and 2000. Can you explain to us the basis for such a comment in your office's reports?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC
utterances.text: Our office dealt with organised return. We dealt with those who submitted applications, who were unable to return based on such applications, and whose return was monitored. Every citizen of Croatia was thus able to come to Croatia, be it from Serbia, or Bosnia and Herzegovina, or from a third country, and was not obliged to report to anyone. Through our field-work, we noted a great number of such returnees, mainly because they applied to international organisations working on the ground to get humanitarian aid or livestock or assistance with household needs. And jointly we reached the number of roughly 20.000 persons who had returned but had not registered. We wanted to register them in order to have them listed as returnees, in order to also give them the official status of returnees so that they could receive some benefits that we were available to provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And I will just inform the Chamber that I would probably have another 30 minutes tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. Mr. Pejkovic, we will adjourn for the day. I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have given already today or testimony still to be given tomorrow or the days to come. Is that clear? Then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn, and we will resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 24th of November, quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 24th day of November, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
